raw_content: {"cards":[{"title":"Storytelling Your Price (and Tiers) Instead of Racing to Cheapest","summary":"Price is a story to narrate on your PDP and offers, not a race to the bottom; design tiers, scarcity and discounts with a deliberate narrative.","use_when":"Setting or defending product pricing, launching a discount or dynamic-pricing policy, or building a tiered offer on a product page.","steps":["Treat price as a story you tell, not just a number. Decide the narrative for every price point on the PDP: what change you promise, who the price is for, and why it is fair.","Run the source's reaction test on your pricing and promotions: how do buyers feel when they get an exclusive discount? When someone else gets it and they don't? Use the answers to choose whether to offer a discount quietly, publicly, or not at all.","Use scarcity and tiered pricing (as on Kickstarter-style campaigns) to build tension that pushes a buyer to act, but ensure the scarcity is real and the tiers have a defined reason for existing.","Avoid defaulting to cheapest. Attributing to the source: racing to be the cheapest usually means you're not investing in change, and 'cheap is another way to say scared' — you promise the same thing, only cheaper, and low price is the last refuge of a marketer out of generous ideas.","Watch the demand-matching failure mode: Tesla's fixed-price story reassured luxury buyers, while Uber's demand-matched pricing cost it brand trust. For your own store, test demand-based pricing only where your customers can articulate the fairness story.","If you charge a premium, make generosity of change, empathy and respect the axis of competition — the source argues customers will pay a lot if you genuinely change them."],"caveats":["The Tesla and Uber outcomes are the source's illustrative examples, not benchmarks for your store.","Scarcity and FOMO tactics depend on real limits; fake scarcity damages the trust you're trying to build."],"tags":["brand","pricing","offer-design","product-page","promotion","positioning","discounts"]},{"title":"Free Ideas, Paid Souvenirs: Structuring Your Giveaway-to-Purchase Ladder","summary":"Give away ideas and content for free to build reach and permission, then monetize the expensive tangible 'souvenir' expressions of those ideas.","use_when":"Deciding what to give away free (content, guides, tools, samples) versus what to charge for in your product line and funnel.","steps":["Split your offering into two married categories: free ideas that spread easily, and expensive expressions of those ideas that are worth paying for.","Make the free layer genuinely free and easy to find, engage with frequently, and share — the source's examples are a chef giving recipes or appearing on podcasts while charging $24 for the plated dish, and free radio songs with $84 concert tickets.","Treat the paid item as a 'souvenir' of the free idea: it should feel worth paying for because it delivers the idea in an elevated, tangible form (china and a tablecloth, a live show).","In an ecommerce context, the free layer might be education, calculators, guides or community content, and the paid layer a physical or service expression of it. The source's demonstrated cases are chef/restaurant and musician/concert, not ecommerce, so treat the mapping as an application, not a proven result.","Do not go fully free: the source gives two reasons — (1) a free transaction loses scarcity, tension and enrollment, and (2) without cash flow you can't invest in product, team or marketing.","Remember free is a different category of transaction, not a penny less: a free idea can spread at effectively infinite scale, but you still need the paid expression to make a living."],"caveats":["The source's free-plus-paid examples come from restaurants and music; the ecommerce version is an adaptation, not a documented ecommerce result."],"tags":["brand","offer-design","content-strategy","monetization","acquisition","funnel"]},{"title":"High Price as a Trust-Building Device (Not a Trust Killer)","summary":"Counterintuitively, large or risky purchases can manufacture trust through cognitive dissonance, so lowering price is not the way to earn confidence.","use_when":"Deciding whether to discount to overcome buyer hesitation on a high-consideration item, membership or premium service.","steps":["Recognize the source's pattern: because a large purchase is risky, cognitive dissonance makes buyers invent trust to justify the commitment ('I'm smart, so I must trust this seller').","Use commitment as an alignment tool. The source points to boot camp, Outward Bound and high-end restaurants that survive bad reviews: heavy investment of cash, reputation or effort makes people align with the choice they made.","Therefore, do not assume a discount buys trust. The source explicitly says lowering your price doesn't make you more trusted — it does the opposite.","For ecommerce, this matters most for high-ticket items and subscriptions: invest in the pre-purchase story, proof and onboarding that support the buyer's justification rather than cutting the price to reduce risk.","Be honest about which risk you are asking buyers to take (money, time, effort, reputation) and design the offer around earning the justification, not around removing all cost.","Balance the two readings: trust is generally required before risky transactions, but the same risk can also generate trust after commitment. Use the second effect to support premium positioning, not to excuse bad products."],"caveats":["This is the author's explanation of a psychological effect, illustrated with examples; it is not a recommendation to raise prices without supporting quality and service."],"tags":["brand","pricing","trust","positioning","retention","high-ticket"]},{"title":"Who Is This Change For: Segmenting by Status, Not Just Demographics","summary":"Before changing price, tipping, packaging or offer structure, decide explicitly who the change excludes and how the customer's status story changes.","use_when":"Rolling out a pricing, packaging, service-model or policy change that will affect existing customers, and choosing which customers you are willing to lose.","steps":["State the change plainly: what is changing, and who is it for. Accept the source's position that a change like this can't be for everyone — some customers will have to be told 'it's not for you, sorry.'","Map how each segment's status is affected. USHG eliminated tipping and raised prices 20 percent to fund parental leave, fair wages and professional treatment; diners who enjoyed status from leaving a big tip lost that thrill, while diners whose worldview is fairness and dignity gained a reason to prefer the restaurant.","Give customers a story they can tell themselves and others about choosing you — a small purchase that signals something larger, as the source describes virtue signaling for hosts choosing USHG.","Answer the source's three questions for your own change: Who is it for? What is it for? How is status changed?","Answer the fourth: 'What will I tell the others?' — if the change gives buyers a shareable reason, it can serve as marketing; if not, expect friction.","For ecommerce, apply this to subscription price increases, bundling shifts, shipping-fee changes and loyalty-tier redesigns: write the customer-facing story for each affected segment before launching."],"caveats":["The 20 percent increase and no-tipping model are USHG's specific case, not a template figure.","Existing customers who value the old status dynamic may leave; budget for that rather than assuming everyone stays."],"tags":["brand","pricing","positioning","customer-research","retention","loyalty","subscrip"]},{"title":"Earn Permission Before You Buy Attention: The Owned-List Rule","summary":"Build an owned permission asset (people who would miss you if you stopped) before leaning on paid ads or platform followers.","use_when":"Deciding where to invest acquisition effort and how to treat email/SMS lists, subscriptions and follower bases.","steps":["Define real permission the source's way: if you stopped showing up, people would be concerned and ask where you went. Presumed, legalistic or fine-print permission doesn't count.","Earn it incrementally like dating: don't ask for the sale at first contact; make a promise ('I will send X'), keep it, and don't expand the usage without agreement.","Make a specific, kept promise the core of your email or SMS program — the source notes Woot's daily sales pitch as a valid permission model because it was the promised deal.","Treat the list as a physical asset: the author says to act as if someone spamming the list to hit a metric had walked out with your laptops.","Prefer owned channels over rented ones. Social platforms are sharecropping: you don't hold permission, the platform does, and it monetizes by charging you to reach people you thought you already had.","Measure and grow the metric the source highlights: how many people would reach out and complain if you didn't send the next message?","Let subscribers choose what they hear and in what format; the internet allows differentiated, opted-in communication."],"caveats":["The source's 70 percent open rate and 33 percent response rate come from Yoyodyne in the 1990s and are not modern benchmarks."],"tags":["brand","retention","email","owned-media","acquisition","permission","customer-research"]},{"title":"Generosity at the Top of the Funnel: Launch to Neophiliacs Without Selling","summary":"Reach the small group of novelty-seeking early adopters with real news and generosity, not a hard pitch, and let them spread the word.","use_when":"Planning a product launch, community seeding or influencer campaign for a brand-new offer with no existing audience.","steps":["Identify the neophiliacs in your category — the people who seek out new voices, ideas and options — and note the source's warning that there aren't many of them, but there may be enough.","Go where those people already gather and have opted in, rather than starting with broad ads. The source's example is Marvel launching at San Diego Comic-Con a year before the film, giving a coming attraction, a director interview and actual news instead of ticket selling.","Be generous rather than promotional at this stage: give attention-worthy content and signal 'this is the sort of thing people like us will be talking about.'","Treat the early phase as earning permission and attention over time, not immediate conversion.","Accept that the size of the early audience doesn't matter; the quality of the story, empathy and generosity does, and word of mouth is the intended output.","Build tension and status into the early experience so early users become connected ambassadors (see the closing lesson of the HugDug case, below)."],[],"caveats":["This is a launch-strategy argument illustrated with film and technology examples; it does not guarantee organic spread.","Early adopters want new and risky; the mass market wants proven and safe, so the same message will not carry you across (see the chasm card)."],"tags":["brand","acquisition","launch","content-strategy","community","early-adopters"]},{"title":"Remarkability Is Decided by Users, So Build Talkability Into the Product","summary":"You cannot declare your store remarkable; users decide, and the best reason they share is because sharing reflects well on them.","use_when":"Designing product, packaging, service or post-purchase moments intended to generate word-of-mouth.","steps":["Build remarkability into the product or service with intent — the source argues effective marketers are therefore in charge of the customer experience, not just the message.","Accept the asymmetry: whether something is remarkable is the user's decision, not yours; if they remark on it, it's remarkable.","Optimize for self-interested sharing: people spread word because it boosts their taste, standing, or desire for novelty and change — 'look at how good my taste is.'","Design the post-purchase moment so the buyer gets a reason to talk: something notable to show, tell or gift.","Avoid stunts. The source explicitly distinguishes stunts (offensive, juvenile, urgent or selfish attention grabs) from genuine remarkability, warning that people reciprocate by shunning and censuring those who cross lines.","Test the rule that even an anti-sharing rule can backfire into sharing — Fight Club's first rule became an invitation to talk — but use that dynamic knowingly, not as a cheap stunt.","For ecommerce specifically: consider the unboxing, the surprise insert, the genuinely novel product feature, or a shareable result the buyer can post; and check whether your own team would bring it up unprompted."],"caveats":["The source gives qualitative reasoning and cultural examples, not measured lift from remarkability in stores."],"tags":["brand","word-of-mouth","product-page","creative-strategy","packaging","customer-experience","differentiation"]},{"title":"Designing Evangelism Into the Offer: Giving Customers a Reason to Tell Others","summary":"People will not spread your word because it matters to you; design the offer so sharing advances the customer's own goals.","use_when":"Building referral mechanics, shareable content, community features or product designs meant to generate peer-to-peer spread.","steps":["Start from the source's premise: ideas travel horizontally, person to person, not from organization to customer, so you must begin with the smallest possible core and give them something to talk about and a reason to do so.","Give people a 'why' to share, not an instruction. The source says it is never the case that people tell friends because you want them to, ask them to, or worked hard — give them a why, and that usually means changing what you offer.","Design the sharer's benefit into the exchange: it furthers their goals and lets them tell a story about themselves they're proud of.","Borrow the AA pattern of generosity: members talk about it as an act of service and a lifeline, not as a promotion — the source calls it a shame killer and a fellowship.","Answer the two bridge questions for any shared item: 'What will I tell my friends?' and 'Why will I tell them?'","In practice for a store: add referral or group-buy mechanics where the sharer's own life improves when a friend joins, and write the customer-facing script so the sharer can tell the story without awkwardness."],"caveats":["The awkwardness of pushing friends to a shopping site is real; the HugDug case shows that even low-effort sharing can fail without tension and a status story."],"tags":["brand","referral","word-of-mouth","community","offer-design","acquisition","retention"]},{"title":"Fixing a Leaky Funnel: Six Levers for Store Conversion","summary":"Treat your funnel as leaky and work six specific levers: right people, aligned promise, fewer steps, support, tension, and a megaphone.","use_when":"Diagnosing where a store or landing-page funnel loses buyers and deciding what to change next.","steps":["Attract the right people at the top rather than maximizing raw traffic volume.","Align the promise that brought the visitor in with the destination you want them to reach — mismatch between what you say and what they hear is a named leak.","Remove steps so fewer decisions are required; note the source's explicit tension here: each extra click makes the funnel more expensive, but remove too many and buyers won't trust you enough to purchase.","Support people as they move through: reinforce their dreams and ameliorate their fears along the way.","Use tension to create forward motion, and recognize that saying yes is often more stressful than walking away — the source says people generally become more distracted, fearful and eager to run away as they progress.","Hand successfully engaged customers a megaphone, a tool to tell the others, completing the 'people like us do things like this' cycle.","Recognize that trust is not static through the funnel; it shifts as people move from stranger to friend to customer to loyal customer."],"caveats":["The source presents this as a framework, not a tested sequence with measured lift per lever."],"tags":["brand","conversion-optimization","checkout","landing-page","funnel","customer-experience","measurement"]},{"title":"Funnel Math with LTV: When Ads Pay and When to Fix the Funnel First","summary":"Do the staged arithmetic from first click to loyal customer, compare acquisition cost with customer lifetime value, and refuse to buy ads you can't trace.","use_when":"Deciding ad budgets and channels, diagnosing an unprofitable paid campaign, or setting the target CAC for a store.","steps":["Lay out the funnel as explicit stages. The source's illustration: spend $1,000 on online ads reaching a million people, get twenty clicks ($50 per click), one in ten of those becomes an order ($500 per order). Recreate this with your own store's numbers before scaling.","Establish the lifetime value of a customer, which the source calls the most important figure to determine. Use the supermarket example as the model: ignore the $1–2 profit on a single trip; a shopper spending $100 twice a week for five years is $50,000+ in sales, about $1,000 profit at 2 percent margin.","Add referral value if regular customers bring in other regulars; the source says this makes each customer more valuable as an engine of growth.","The buy-rule from the source's direct-mail framing: if stamps cost 50 cents and you need 1,000 letters per order, each order costs $500. If LTV is $700, buy as many as you can; if LTV is $400, you have no business buying them — get a better letter or a better business.","Apply the source's two hard rules: if you can't see the funnel, don't buy the ads; if you can measure it and it still costs too much, don't buy the ads — fix the funnel first.","Optimize for step shifting and elimination and for lifetime value rather than only shaving cost per click. Lowering CPC with a ridiculous ad promise backfires: trust drops once buyers are inside and yield plummets."],"caveats":["The source notes google/facebook take roughly half of online ad spend and skim much of the advertiser's profit; margins here are illustrative.","Numbers are the author's examples (and a rough 2018 estimate that about 60 percent of advertisers measure results); use your own data."],"tags":["brand","measurement","acquisition","customer-acquisition-cost","lifetime-value","funnel","paid-ads"]},{"title":"Why Magical Self-Running Funnels Are Rare — Build the Post-Click Cohort","summary":"Most funnels cannot be passive profit machines; use ads to prime the pump, then build trust, trial, and a cohort that stays.","use_when":"Evaluating the promise of an automated or passive acquisition system, and deciding how much effort to put after the first click.","steps":["Reject the passive-funnel fantasy. The source says these magical funnels are rare because the lifetime value of a new customer rarely exceeds the cost of ads to acquire them, given distrust and web clutter.","Adopt the source's operating model: prime the pump with ads aimed at neophiliacs, then build trust with frequency, gain trial, generate word of mouth, and make it pay with a cohort that needs your work to be part of who they are.","Put disproportionate effort into what happens after the first click, which the source calls the easy thing to skip and the expensive part to neglect.","Accept that most thriving brands are primed by advertising but built by good marketing — users evangelizing to friends, and communities coalescing around cultural change.","Avoid pushing too hard and too fast to force perpetual motion; the source says that ends in bitterness because it can't last.","For a store: budget for retention, repeat purchase and community alongside paid acquisition, and judge new customer cohorts by whether they return, not just by first-order ROAS."],"caveats":["The source's claims about funnel economics are opinions and examples, and include an aside that he is unsure why funnel math confuses people; verify against your own P&L."],"tags":["brand","retention","measurement","paid-ads","lifetime-value","funnel","cohorts"]},{"title":"Trust Through Action: What You Do Outweighs What You Say","summary":"In a low-trust environment, buyers remember what you did long after they forget what you said, so invest in service actions, not messaging.","use_when":"Handling refunds, defective products, data problems, fulfillment errors or any moment when the store's behavior is visible to a customer.","steps":["Choose your path deliberately. The source says marketers land in one of three places: ignored, sneaking around, or trusted — and only trust pays for the investment.","Commit to the third path: make a promise and keep it, earning enrollment, then attention, then the ability to tell a story, then more trust and word of mouth.","Favor doing over talking. The source asks the concrete test: when a customer asked for a refund on a defective product, what did you do? When you lost data, what did you do?","Focus on what you do when no one is watching, one person at a time, day by day — rather than a press conference for the masses.","Recognize that benefit of the doubt is scarce and is only granted when people are already heading where they think you're going and their identity and status are on the line.","Apply it to fulfillment and support policy: the source's supermarket reasoning implies it is hardly worth a thousand dollars in lost lifetime sales to argue over a four-dollar unripe melon. Set refund and return thresholds accordingly."],"caveats":["The supermarket example is the source's illustration of LTV logic, not a universal refund policy; set your own threshold from your LTV data."],"tags":["brand","trust","retention","customer-service","returns","fulfillment","lifetime-value"]},{"title":"Famous to the Smallest Viable Audience, Not the Biggest Number","summary":"Aim to be known to a small, right-sized tribe (the source's 'fifteen hundred to three thousand people') rather than maximizing follower counts.","use_when":"Deciding where to concentrate brand and PR effort, and how to measure community reach versus raw audience size.","steps":["Adopt the source's framing: everyone is famous to about fifteen hundred people, some to three thousand, and for a consultant, designer or inventor, being famous to the right three thousand is plenty.","Define your smallest viable audience — the number and type of people who make the business work — and aim your store's marketing at them rather than at everyone.","Use fame functionally: it breeds trust partly because people your buyers already trust have heard of you. Prioritize credibility within the tribe over broad reach.","Choose public relations over publicity. The source distinguishes public relations (telling your story to the right people in the right way) from a publicist chasing clips, and warns against ink at all costs.","Treat the peer-to-peer trust transferred through trusted voices as the goal, and be aware the author expects the value of broad fame to fade over time as more people become famous."],"caveats":["The 1,500–3,000 figures are the author's heuristics, not computed audience benchmarks."],"tags":["brand","positioning","audience","publicity","community","trust"]},{"title":"The Chasm: Why Early Buyers Won't Carry You to the Mass Market","summary":"Early adopters want new and risky while the mass market wants safe and proven, so plan a bridge instead of assuming the first group will spread the word.","use_when":"Planning category entry, product-market expansion or launch sequencing when early-adopter traction has not converted into mainstream sales.","steps":["Recognize the gap Geoff Moore named in the Rogers adoption curve: early adopters buy new, interesting, slightly risky things because that is what they like, and there aren't enough of them to build a mass business.","Understand why the crossing so often fails: satisfying early adopters may require annoying the masses, because the very thing your product did (break the pattern) is what the mass market does not want. The source's illustration is watching the help desk at an Apple store — the middle of the curve is barely adapting.","Build the bridge on network effects. The source's rule: people won't talk about your new chocolate because friends eating it doesn't improve their life, but they will talk about a communication app because their life improves when friends join.","Answer the two questions the bridge rests on: what will I tell my friends, and why will I tell them? Then change what you offer so the answer is a real incentive, not a request.","Expect the Gartner hype trough — neophiliacs get bored and the mass market disdains you — and treat that moment as when you most need a bridge story matched to a more conservative worldview.","For a store, ask whether your product creates ratchet value for the buyer when neighbors or coworkers adopt it; if not, plan a different bridge (proof, safety, pattern-matching) rather than relying on viral spread."],"caveats":["The source frames this as Moore's chasm applied to marketing generally; specifics about which stores can bridge it are your application, not documented results."],"tags":["brand","positioning","adoption","network-effects","launch","word-of-mouth","strategy"]},{"title":"Crossing the Local Chasm: Yo-Yos, Facebook and Village Water","summary":"Crossing doesn't require a global leap — a well-seeded local adoption with low entry cost and identity can change everything.","use_when":"Seeding a product in a specific community, campus, niche or region before attempting broader rollout.","steps":["Seed with the right early adopter, not the first volunteer. In the source's schoolyard example, the first kid with the yo-yo was the wrong kid on the wrong day; weeks later a charismatic fifth-grader founded the Yo-yo Union, was skilled but not intimidating, and brought three more yo-yos for friends who were each leaders in their own right.","Keep entry cost low and the payoff quick, so a core forms fast — the source describes thirty kids within a week and the whole school soon after.","Then add stickiness. The source notes yo-yos cooled off as fast as they spread, while Uggs, black backpacks and penny skateboards persisted because of identity and persistence.","Select local tribes where insecure, status-seeking, well-connected members already gather; the source's Facebook reading is that it started at Harvard with students who had urgent status needs, fast connections, spare time and a desire to be seen.","Make the early product a badge and a conversation starter. In the Water Health International case, the brightly colored jerry cans signaled adoption and invited conversation.","Use vivid local demonstration to shift habit, as WHI does by bringing a microscope projector into classrooms so children see the germs and parasites in their own household water samples — the source says changing a multigenerational habit takes time even with obvious benefits."],"caveats":["Facebook's and WHI's outcomes are case illustrations; the author also warns that the final leap to a huge mass market is unlikely for most marketers."],"tags":["brand","launch","community","adoption","positioning","local-marketing","network-effects"]},{"title":"Divide the Market into Short Heads: Escaping the Long-Tail Trap","summary":"Being one obscure item on an infinite shelf rarely pays; create the definitive hit for a defined niche so you become its short head.","use_when":"Choosing product selection strategy, niche assortment breadth, or deciding whether to compete as a tiny seller on a giant marketplace.","steps":["Understand the shape from the source: hits on the left each sell enormously, while the long tail doesn't sell much per item but collectively equals the short head — half of Amazon's book sales are titles outside the top five thousand.","Accept the economics honestly. The source's stark warning is that these marketplaces depend on the hopes of individuals far out on the long tail: the internet can live on tiny slices, but you can't.","Recognize that aggregating the tail can work. The April Fools'/Passover/Easter/birthday T-shirt would sell about four units alone, but companies making tens of thousands of print-on-demand designs together sell thousands per month.","If you are not aggregating, take the way out: build the definitive, most essential, extraordinary contribution to your field, and connect the market so they see you belong in the short head.","Name your niche market explicitly (the source lists teen literary fiction, chip carving, GH5 filmmaking, improv) and make the hit that serves as glue: the DeWalt hammer drill and Rocky Horror are cited as things that unite 'people like us.'","For product selection, ask both questions: does this item create or dominate a short head for a defined audience, and does it help that audience recognize each other?","Treat outlier success stories as wishes, not strategies — the source says becoming an outlier isn't a strategy."],"caveats":["The Amazon halves and T-shirt volume are the source's illustrative numbers, not audited data."],"tags":["brand","product-selection","niche","positioning","assortment","differentiation","marketplaces"]},{"title":"Learning From HugDug's Failure: Trial Without Whales and Tension Dies","summary":"A cautionary case from the source: thousands of pages were built but almost no 'whales' promoted them, because tension and status incentives were missing.","use_when":"Designing a user-generated, community, referral or affiliate program and setting realistic time-to-traction expectations.","steps":["Review what HugDug did: users could build a page profiling an Amazon product in about four minutes, with a royalty split to charity; the bet was that authors would promote their own books and Pinterest-style users would build pages at scale.","Look at the failure pattern honestly: they got trial (thousands of pages) but fewer than six people built more than a dozen pages or promoted them much; tension dissipated after a single visit with no reason to return, and many pages sold zero books in a month.","Diagnose the three named causes and check your own program against them: insufficient incentives, no tension dynamic turning early users into connected ambassadors, and no status story.","Also note the stated difficulty: it remains emotionally hard to push friends to a shopping site even when it is technically easy.","Apply the fix to your program design: be specific about who your first customers are and what they might want, believe and say; create a status story; and build a reason to return repeatedly.","Set realistic timelines — the source's team concluded they were naive to think four months was enough to create an overnight success, and calls a Kickstarter-like success harder than it looks."],"caveats":["This is the author's own failed venture, presented as a lesson; the causes are his diagnosis, not an independently verified post-mortem."],"tags":["brand","referral","community","retention","customer-research","status","program-design"]},{"title":"Casey Neistat's Funnel Numbers: Reading Stage Conversions Realistically","summary":"A worked example of a large-permission-asset funnel: roughly 1,000,000 views to 18,000 to 1,000 to 5, showing steep attrition at each step.","use_when":"Setting realistic expectations for a content-to-conversion funnel and deciding which stage to improve.","steps":["Use the source's chain as a mental model for your own staged funnel: about one in fifty viewers clicked from YouTube to the Twitch stream (10M+ views, 1M seen at the time, 18,000 on the stream).","Then about one in eighteen of those stream viewers posted a comment (roughly 1,000 comments), and of those, perhaps five took a further action such as signing up.","Apply this in a store: measure each transition separately (content view → product page click → add to cart → purchase → repeat) rather than only the endpoints, and expect steep attrition between each.","Note the source's own diagnosis of what makes this work: the reason isn't funnel optimization, it's that the top is regularly and effortlessly filled with people already enrolled in his journey.","Prioritize strengthening the top-of-funnel enrollment and the trust behind it over micro-optimizing deep stages, since the source says everything gets better once you earn that trust.","Use exact numbers for your own funnel, treating these as an illustrative shape rather than a benchmark."],"caveats":["These are the author's approximate, single-observation numbers from one creator at one time, explicitly 'your mileage may vary,' and are not benchmarks for stores."],"tags":["brand","funnel","measurement","content-strategy","conversion-optimization","audience","metrics"]}]}

input.source_name: This Is Marketing_ You Can’t Be Seen Until You Learn to Se (1).docx
input.text:
On one hand, you can tell the story that the price is the price. Tesla told this story to luxury car buyers and they breathed a sigh of relief. But when Uber tried to match pricing to demand, it cost their brand billions in trust. For most organizations, particularly small ones, the hard part isn’t the mechanics of charging different amounts. It’s the storytelling. It’s the storytelling. I bring this up because it’s a powerful way to understand the story of your price (and the price of your story). How do you feel when you find out that you got a discount that no one else got? What if you deserved it? How do you feel if other people got that discount and you didn’t? What about the scarcity and pricing built into Kickstarter? Does the fear of missing out on a level that’s almost full push you to act? “Cheap” is another way to say “scared” Unless you’ve found an extraordinary new way to deliver your service or product, racing to be the cheapest probably means that you’re not investing sufficiently in change. When you’re the cheapest, you’re not promising change. You’re promising the same, but cheaper. The race to the bottom is tempting, because nothing is easier to sell than cheaper.

 It requires no new calculations or deep thinking on the part of your customer. It’s not cultural or emotional. It’s simply cheaper. Low price is the last refuge of a marketer who has run out of generous ideas. And what about free? If marketing is done for and with the consumer, why not make everything free? Two reasons: 1. Engaging in a transaction is fundamentally different than encountering an apparently worthless (or at least priceless) object that’s been freely shared. Scarcity, tension, and enrollment all exist when we must decide to make a purchase, and the marketer sacrifices all of these when a purchase is truly free. 2. Without cash flow, you can’t invest in your product, your team, or your marketing. But free is worth considering for other reasons, in other situations. Free is not simply a penny less than a penny, a dollar less than a dollar. It’s an entirely different category of transaction, because like dividing by zero, it scales to infinity. A free idea is far more likely to spread, and spread quickly, than an idea that’s A free idea is far more likely to spread, and spread quickly, than an idea that’s tethered to money. If Facebook cost three dollars a month to use, it would have attracted fewer than a million users. If it cost money to listen to the hits on the radio, the Top 40 would disappear. And yet . . . We don’t know how to make a living if we give everything away. The road out of this paradox is to combine two offerings, married to each other: 1. Free ideas that spread. 2. Expensive expressions of those ideas that are worth paying for. When a chef gives away her recipes, or appears on a podcast, or leads an online seminar, she’s giving her ideas away for free. It’s easy to find them, engage with them with frequency, and share them. But, if you want to eat that pasta served on china on a white tablecloth at her restaurant, it’s going to cost you twenty-four dollars. When a song on the radio is free, but the concert ticket costs eighty-four dollars, the artist can be compensated. The china and the ticket are souvenirs of ideas, and souvenirs are supposed to be expensive. There are countless ways for you to share your vision, your ideas, your digital expressions, your ability to connect—for free. And each of them builds awareness, permission, and trust, which gives you a platform to sell the thing that’s worth paying for. Trust and risk, trust and expense The rational thing is to believe that we’re more likely to require trust before we engage in risky transactions. And it’s also rational to expect that people are more likely to want more trust before spending a lot of money (a form of risk). Or committing time and effort. Many times, though, the opposite is true. The fact that the transaction is risky causes cognitive dissonance to kick in. In 2016, they stunned a lot of observers by eliminating tipping. Instead of accepting tips, USHG raised their prices 20 percent. They devoted the increased revenue to offering parental leave, fair wages, and the chance to treat their team as professionals. The shift meant that the folks in the back of the house (who actually cook your food) get paid better, and it means that the waitstaff have an incentive to work together, to trade shifts, to work the way a doctor, a pilot, or a teacher might—for the work, not for a tip. How do you communicate the price increase and elimination of tipping to a regular customer, someone who values the perception of a special relationship because he sees himself as an above-average tipper? How to communicate this to a tourist, who is comparing menu prices online before making a reservation, and doesn’t know that having tips included makes the restaurant much cheaper than it appears? If you’re at the circle, or worse, to the right of that circle, you can’t compete for impact or ad dollars, because even though Google profits from every website they search, most of the people out on the edges are huffing and puffing. These huge marketplaces (Amazon, Netflix, iTunes, etc.) depend on the misguided hopes and dreams of individuals way out on the long tail. Separately, each one struggles. Taken together, it’s a good business. Traffic to the most popular websites The April Fools’ Passover Birthday Easter shirt Here’s a vivid example of living on the long tail: The other day I saw a T-shirt for sale on Amazon that said “It’s Easter, It’s Passover, It’s April Fools’, and It’s My Birthday.” That’s obviously a special-interest item, one that can’t possibly support the effort that went into it. After all, only one in 365 people qualifies to wear a shirt like that, and perhaps one in a thousand of those would actually wear one, and, I don’t know, perhaps one in a hundred of their friends would think to search for it, so the vendor probably sold four. But there it was. More searching found shirts like this one: Oh, I see. It’s a long-tail business. A few companies are making tens of thousands of different shirts. They’re making them to order. The long tail and the infinite shelf space of Amazon makes this possible. They might not sell many (any) of any particular shirt, but taken together, it’s reasonable to assume that they’re selling thousands of shirts a month. If you can aggregate a chunk of the long tail, you can make a go of it. But you can’t possibly sell just one obscure shirt and have a shot. This is the false promise of the internet. That you can be happy with a tiny slice of the long tail. That anyone can sing or write or dance or do comedy or coach or freelance, and so anyone will, and so you’ll be fine. Except you won’t be fine, because you can’t live on that. The internet can live on that, Upwork and Fiverr and Netflix and Amazon can live on that, but you can’t. We hear about the outliers, the kids who make millions of dollars a year with We hear about the outliers, the kids who make millions of dollars a year with their YouTube channel or the fashionista with millions of followers. But becoming an outlier isn’t a strategy. It’s a wish. There’s a way out The math of a hit is about more than the benefit of selling a lot of copies. Actually, hits are hits because people like hits. We like to do what everyone else is doing. (Everyone means “everyone like us.”) You’ve probably guessed the strategy: by dividing the market into many curves, not just one, we end up with many short heads and many long tails. There’s the market for literary fiction aimed at teenagers. The market for books on chip carving. The market for video courses on using a GH5 camera to make movies. And the market for performing improv. There’s even the market for drone music played so loudly that the audience needs to wear ear protection. In each of these markets, and a million others, there’s a need for a short head, at least once someone has connected the people in that market to one another, so they realize that they exist, so they see each other, and so they understand what the hit is. Because it’s the hit that connects them. Once they see it, they’ll probably want it. This means that living on the long tail has two essential elements: 1. Creates the definitive, the most essential, the extraordinary contribution to the field. 2. Connects the market you’ve designed it for, and helps them see that you belong in the short head. That this hit is the glue that holds them together. Rocky Horror is in the short head. So is the DeWalt 20V Max XR lithium ion brushless hammer drill. It’s the hit that unites us. The one that makes it clear that you are people like us. Yes, the internet is a discovery tool. But no, you’re not going to get discovered that way. Instead, you will make your impact by uniting those you seek to serve. Instead, you will make your impact by uniting those you seek to serve. Bridging the chasm We have no idea who discovered the pothole, or who named the Grand Canyon, but Geoff Moore discovered the chasm. It’s the overlooked but often fatal gap in the Rogers curve, the curve of how ideas spread through the culture. The early adopters go first; they buy things because they’re new, interesting, and a little bit risky. They do that because they like things that are new, interesting, and little bit risky. But there’s a problem. There aren’t enough of these neophiliacs to go around. Big organizations, mass movements, and substantial profits often depend on the mass market—they need action from the rest of us. The mass market is where Heinz and Starbucks and JetBlue and The American Heart Association and Amazon and a hundred others live. How do you get there? The intuitive answer is that the early adopters will bring your idea to the masses and you’ll be done. But often, that’s not what happens. It doesn’t happen because the mass market wants something different from what the early adopters want. The mass market wants something that works. Something safe. A pattern match, not a pattern interrupt. They take “people like us do things like this” very seriously. Moore’s point was that few innovations glide from one part of the market to the other. That’s because in order to satisfy the early adopters, you may just need to annoy the masses. The very thing your innovation did (break things) is the one thing that the mass market doesn’t want to happen. They don’t want to trade in their DVDs. They don’t want to learn a new software platform. They don’t want to read their news online. To understand how this collision feels, go spend an hour or two at the help desk at the Apple store. Check out who’s there and why. Listen to their questions, and pay attention to their facial expressions. The middle of the curve isn’t eagerly adopting. They’re barely adapting. That’s why they’ve chosen to be in the middle of the curve. Where’s your bridge? Where’s your bridge? The bridge across the chasm lies in network effects. Most of the fast-growing marketing successes of our lifetime have spread because of ideas that work better when everyone knows them. The early adopters have a huge incentive to bring your idea across the chasm to the masses; it will make their lives better if everyone in their network also uses this idea. There’s no reason to talk about a new kind of chocolate you really like. It doesn’t make your life better if others eat it. On the other hand, you spend a lot of time telling people about Snapchat or Instagram or Twitter, because if your friends followed you, your life would improve. That’s the simple ratchet power of network effects. Connected tribes are more powerful than disconnected ones. Individuals who get in early have an incentive to bring others along, and so they do. It’s not just technology, of course, although it is often the force behind the pattern interrupts that have remade our culture. There’s an incentive for me to organize a bus trip to Washington, D.C., to protest gun violence. If more people come, not only will we make more of an impact, but the day will be more fun as well. There’s an incentive to get your friends to sign up for the local CSA farm share. The farmers can’t afford to come for just a few people in the neighborhood, but if lots of people come, there will be better variety for all of us. The peer-to-peer movement of ideas is how we cross the chasm—by giving people a network effect that makes the awkwardness of pitching change worth the effort. The bridge is built on two simple questions: 1. What will I tell my friends? 2. Why will I tell them? It is never the case that people will tell their friends because you want them to, or because you ask them to, or because you worked hard. Give them a why. And that usually involves changing what you offer. Make things better by making better things—things that have a network effect, a ratchet, a reason for sharing. Surviving the chasm The Gartner Hype Cycle is a brilliant meta-analysis of how the culture changes. The technology trigger opens the door for your art, for the contribution you want to make. It interrupts a pattern. The Gartner Hype Cycle In that moment, marketing can help you reach the neophiliacs. Inevitably, these early adopters will hype your work. Of course they will. That’s one of the best reasons to be an early adopter. When the idea is presented to the rest of the market, it can’t possibly compare to the hype. Hence the trough. This is another way to see Moore’s chasm. It’s in this moment, when the neophiliacs are bored with you and the mass market disdains you, that you will most likely lose momentum. This is the moment when you need a bridge, a new way to step through the culture with stories that match the worldviews of this new, more conservative market. And then, with generous persistence, you can walk up the slope to the new plateau, the place where you are now indispensable to the masses. A new pattern replacing the old one. You might not find the bridge Years ago, my team at Squidoo launched hugdug.com. The idea behind HugDug was pretty simple: You could build a page (it took about four minutes) profiling any product on Amazon that you loved. If you chose a book, for example, the page would bring in the cover, the title, and a big button with a link. You’d add your own review and a bunch of relevant content. If someone found the page and bought the book, Amazon would pay us a royalty, and we’d send half of it to your favorite charity. (This was years before smile.amazon.com, and we were donating twenty times as much to charity as they do.) Our bet was that authors would happily promote their books in this way—it was easier to control than their Amazon page, and they could have pride in ownership in how the information was presented, not to mention the philanthropy of it all. We also hoped that the typical Pinterest fan would find a page like this not only fun to build, but gratifying, because they’d be helping to raise money for a cause they cared about. Our thesis was that we’d be able to put in the work to find the early adopters, neophiliacs eager to give shiny new things on the internet a try. We were betting that once they saw that it was working, they’d do it more, moving us deeper along the long tail, generating thousands of pages. And that as the word spread, we’d bring in authors, and they’d be whales, promoting their books like crazy. And that people who saw any of our HugDug pages would not only buy at the same rate they’d be buying on Amazon (after all, it was the same price), but would build their own pages (raising their status because they were sharing insights among an elite crowd, all in service of philanthropy). We kept at it for months, but we failed. I think the main reason we failed was that while we got trial (thousands of pages were built), we failed to find any whales. There were fewer than six people who built more than a dozen pages or promoted them very much. The tension dissipated too quickly. People felt like they had no good reason to return after a single visit. The long tail was so long that it wasn’t unusual for a HugDug page to sell zero books in a month. And most people were hesitant to HugDug page to sell zero books in a month. And most people were hesitant to promote a page, because even though it’s easier now, it’s still emotionally difficult to push your friends to visit a shopping site online. The lesson was that a Kickstarter-like success is always more difficult than it looks. We were naïve in believing that four months was enough time to create an overnight success. We underestimated how difficult it might be to create sufficient incentives, and, most of all, we failed to create a tension dynamic that would have turned our early users into connected ambassadors who would have turned the ratchet as we crossed the chasm. We didn’t do enough to tell a story about status, and we weren’t nearly specific enough about who our first customers would be, what they might have wanted, believed, and said. Case Study: Facebook and crossing the biggest chasm In our lifetime, very few brands have crossed over fully to the mass market. Starbucks, which is familiar to most people reading this, hasn’t made it all the way, and neither has Heineken or even the bagel. But Facebook has. This graph shows what that looks like: Each bar is users during a given year (the month changed midway, but the idea is the same). Sometime around 2008, a whole new bunch of everyone started using Facebook. That leap happened because the reason for signing up changed from “this is sort of interesting” to “this will help me immeasurably” to “I’m the last person on earth who’s not using this.” Starting at Harvard was part of the secret. The insecure Harvard student had an urgent status need: to find out where he or she stood in the pecking order. As it spread through the Ivy League, Facebook crossed one local chasm after As it spread through the Ivy League, Facebook crossed one local chasm after another. At each school, a neophiliac went first (because they like going first) but the relentless ratchet of status kept it spreading. The more friends you had on Facebook, the higher your status. The other people already on Facebook had a status you admired (other Ivy League students). Facebook was planted in the best possible spot, surrounded by insecure, high-status young people, with fast internet connections, plenty of spare time, and an insatiable desire to be seen, to connect, and to move up in some invisible hierarchy. Once it spread through that local tribe, it wasn’t hard to jump to other colleges, and then, finally, the public. This last chasm leap is the billion-dollar one. And once again, status roles kick in. Because Facebook was able to combine nerdiness with status, they were able to surround the middle of the market and create an irresistible ratchet. Join in, or face your worst fear—be socially isolated. As much as most marketers would like to make this last huge leap, it’s unlikely. The market is just too big, and the typical network effect isn’t that strong. Crossing the local chasm The good news is that you don’t need to set out to cross a global chasm. A local one can change everything. The local elementary school is a fine example. One kid brings in a yo-yo on Monday. But he’s the wrong kid on the wrong day. A few weeks later, a charismatic fifth-grader brings in her yo-yo, announcing that she’s starting the Yo-yo Union, an exclusive club that’s open to all. She’s pretty good at tricks, but not so good that she’s intimidating. And she brings three more yo-yos with her, for her friends. Pretty soon, the four of them are out on the playground, walking dogs and sleeping. She’s chosen wisely—each of these early adopters is a leader in her own right. A week later, there are thirty kids with yo-yos on the playground. The cost of entry is low, the payoff is quick, and the connection feels real. A week later, it seems like the whole school is doing it. Because yo-yos are a fad, without stickiness, they cool off as fast as they spread. Of course, it doesn’t have to be that way if you build in identity and persistence. The same crossing happened with Uggs, with black backpacks, with penny skateboards. skateboards. We only notice the ones that cross a local chasm, but the early adopters are always experimenting around the edges. It’s when the combination of adoption and network effects creates enough tension for the idea to cross the local chasm that we notice it. Clean water in a local village For the lucky and privileged, clean water is a given. We’ve never known any other form of water. For a billion people around the world, though, the norm is dirty water, infested with parasites. Often requiring a walk of several hours to fetch, this water is essential for life, but it also makes people sick. Consider the case of Water Health International. When WHI arrives in a village with its water purification kiosk, a few residents immediately understand the possibility for impact. They buy a special Jerry can from WHI and then pay to have it refilled every day. The few pennies spent on clean water are quickly earned back in time saved, increased productivity, and reduced medical expense. And yet, not everyone buys the water right away. Most people don’t. In fact, it follows precisely the same adoption curve as just about everything else, from toys to computers. The early adopters buy it first. They may be educated enough to realize how powerful an input clean water is, but it’s more likely that they simply like buying things that are new. Not only are these early adopters eager to go first, but they’re eager to talk about their experience. The brightly colored water jugs that WHI requires (so they know that they’re not refilling an infected vessel) are a badge of honor and an invitation to converse. But still, the early days are always fairly slow. Changing a multigenerational habit that’s as close to survival as water is does not happen right away. Still, the early adopters won’t stop talking about it. It’s not a fad; fresh water is needed daily, forever. And water is an easy thing to share and talk about. To further the local shift, WHI sends representatives to the local school. Outfitted with a microscope projector, the rep works with the teacher and has each student bring in some water samples from their home. Projecting the samples on the wall, the microscope tells a vivid story that resonates with the eight-year-olds in the class. This is what germs look like. This is what parasites look like.
